questions.prompt: In which Go version were generics (type parameters) added?
questions.explanation: Generics and the `any` alias for `interface{}` arrived in Go 1.18.

questions.prompt: What does the `comparable` constraint permit that `any` does not?
questions.explanation: `comparable` allows equality comparison (needed for map keys and `==` checks); `any` allows neither operators nor comparisons.

questions.prompt: Can a method declare its own type parameters?

options.text: No — a method may only use the type parameters of its receiver type
Yes — any method can add type parameters

questions.explanation: Methods cannot introduce new type parameters; they may only use the ones declared on the receiver type.

questions.prompt: In a constraint, `~float64` matches any type whose ____ type is float64.
questions.explanation: The ~ approximation matches any type whose underlying type is the given one, so `type Celsius float64` satisfies `~float64`.

questions.prompt: When are generics the right tool? Select all that apply.

options.text: One algorithm applied across many types with the same operations
A type-safe container like a stack or set

questions.explanation: Generics fit shared algorithms and type-safe containers to remove duplication; when types have different behaviors you want to dispatch on, use an interface instead.

questions.prompt: Match each generics term to its meaning.

pairs.right: A placeholder type in brackets like [T any]
An interface limiting which types are allowed
The compiler deducing type arguments from the call

questions.explanation: Type parameters are constrained by interfaces; `any` is the unrestricted constraint; inference usually fills in the type arguments.
